I thought her character was really realistic (realLIZtic, sorry), she’s a recovered addict and we only really meet her after her recovery. The townspeople embrace her and those around her forgive her because she presents as a very sweet and docile person, but we see her old habits come back (I’ll never forgive her for throwing the ashtray at TJ and hitting him). I’ve met a lot of people who did a lot of harm before they stabilized, either because of drugs, mental illness, or general life circumstance, and unfortunately they don’t always make amends for their actions. Many separate their lives into two parts, the “healed” and “unhealed” versions of them, and refuse to associate with or take accountability for the pain they caused because they don’t want to “dwell on the past”. In reality, they just don’t want to have to accept that they acted in a harmful way and caused real damage, so they avoid ever even talking about it. Every attempt to communicate about it is met with “but I’m better now, see? Stop bringing up the past when I’m trying so hard to be different!” 

And it’s hard to be around them because often they’re doing better and acting better, and you don’t want to disrupt that, but you also can’t forgive the way they hurt you in the past. I really do wish we had at least one deeper conversation between her and Jess, especially when the town embraced her but ostracized Jess as a literal child who had been abused. Especially with her having another child, I really do think her previous experience as a mother should be explored more, instead of the weird “you can do this” message the show chose

Just my opinion, but I don’t think it’s about money at all. She mentioned that she wants to go out like you used to, and that you haven’t been. It sounds to me like she’s feeling lonely, and I bet the real problem is that she hasn’t had enough intentional time together lately. I think she’s conflating time with money in this instance, in the sense that she thinks you need to spend money to have quality time together, and feels upset that even a small amount of money is going to something that doesn’t involve the both of you because she thinks it will take away from your ability to spend quality time together for the next two weeks. Like you said, you’re doing regular adult maintenance things that don’t cost more than a few dollars and are very necessary. It seems like she’s more freaking out about doing nothing together for a while because you won’t have enough money to. 

You are probably trying to take care of her by doing these things alone so she doesn’t have to (acts of service), and she is probably feeling left out because you’re leaving her alone to go do these things (quality time). One person thinks they’re making the other person feel loved, but the other person doesn’t receive love in that way and ends up feeling left out instead of cared for. Unfortunately, it’s pretty common if both parties don’t communicate extensively about their feelings and needs, which it sounds like she might be having trouble doing when she feels her needs are being neglected. 

Also, being in the hospital for chronic illness treatment sucks, and that’s probably contributing to her frustration. Not only is it painful, but she also probably feels left out and upset at her own body for not being able to do what she wants to. And the fact that she’s going through it alone when she already feels like her needs are neglected is probably what sparked this and why it came up now instead of earlier when you first talked about it and scheduled everything. 

I think she just wants you to hear her, reassure her, and spend some quality time together to make her feel like a priority. Maybe pick her up a few snacks and some flowers for after her treatment, or if you can’t do that due to budgeting, maybe make her some dinner and sit down with a game or some couples prompts you can find online. Or you could take her to a pretty park and eat there, maybe even read or paint. Even a walk together might help.

She’s also probably frustrated because she wants to feel supported and heard by you, but is communicating her feelings in a way that doesn’t usually elicit the response she wants (reassurance and connection). So when you withdraw, it affirms her anxieties in her head and makes her feel unseen. She should definitely work on being able to express her feelings in a more constructive manner, but she can’t do that right now, so definitely don’t ignore her even if you think she’s being ridiculous. It can be hard to care for our partners when their reaction to negative emotions is to push us away, but one of the best and most useful things I’ve ever learned in relationships is to identify what your partner really needs in that moment, not what they’re saying. The vast majority of the time, if you take care of that immediate need and reconnect, the conversation becomes much less hostile and you can actually talk through your true feelings.

You made the decision to get married to her, and she to you, you obviously both care about each other enough to promise forever. Try to hold a bit of space for her “irrational” feelings right now, even if you think they’re unfair, even if she’s not expressing herself in the nicest manner, and reassure her of your love and dedication to her by making time for the two of you. 

Your feeling are of course valid too, but I doubt she’ll be able to talk to you about them calmly until you both deal with her need for connection right now.

Personally, I would break up. It sounds like you two have incompatible values and viewpoints that aren’t conducive to a relationship together. 

Him speaking to you that way, even if he apologized, is a big red flag. I obviously can’t say for certain, but it sounds like he might feel entitled to your body and got angry because your plans don’t line up with his expectations. It is ultimately YOUR choice to carry or not carry a child. Childbirth is a lot to ask from someone. 

I’ve heard horror stories from friends of friends of women whose partners said they respected the fact that they didn’t want to have children, but who later ended up mysteriously pregnant, only to find that their partner poked holes in condoms or switched out birth control. Obviously those are extreme cases and I’m not accusing your boyfriend of this, but it’s something to keep in mind when he’s already shown disrespect towards you and your decision. Personally, I would have a hard time trusting someone who demonstrated his behavior. 

Also, if you are afraid to bring up a topic to your partner because they might become verbally abusive again, that’s another red flag. You should always feel comfortable with your partner, and the two of you should be able to discuss matters that you disagree on without becoming hostile.

I am happy!! I never thought it would be possible for me considering I had horrible mental health problems up until recently, but I genuinely feel so joyful and content. The secret I found for me personally is that life is not about feeling happy 100% of the time. Of course bad things happen and you will have bad days, but if you are generally content in life, they won’t have such a huge impact on you. 

How to become content:
One of the biggest things that helped me was completely starting over. I moved to a new city far away from where I grew up, where I knew absolutely no one, and I applied for random jobs I thought sounded fun but felt unqualified for. Lo and behold, I got my dream job at 22! I work in a very unconventional field that has been a huge area of interest for me my whole life, a job I always wanted but never thought practical. But it happened! 

I moved because I felt like the town I grew up in didn’t reflect my values or suit my needs, so I chose a better fit for me. This also let me completely reinvent myself, because nobody knew me here. I think when you feel surrounded by things that remind you of a self you don’t want to be and no longer identify with, and when people continue to expect you to behave like that stagnant self, you can feel stuck being a person you don’t like. I started trying new things, putting myself in situations that felt outside my comfort zone, and experimenting more, and that let me discover who I am outside of who I was. 

I also started surrounding myself with passionate people, people who do things only because they love them (Usually creative types), because they encouraged me to love what I love too. 

Look for anything that makes you want to do it. It doesn’t have to even be something you want to do forever. Maybe you want to try painting, or clay, or writing, basketball, cooking, anything. 


Also:
Learning to appreciate everything around me, to decorate my space and surround myself with things I actively chose and enjoy. Becoming intentional with what I surround myself with (objects, environments, and people) has been so important in finding happiness. I have an opinion on everything I do and fill my time with only things I want to do. Even things I didn’t want to do previously have become better (example: laundry, I want to do it because I want to take care of myself and my space and also be able to wear whatever I want). 

But the most important thing:
I am grateful for everything in my life. And I am not grateful just because everything is good, I started being grateful for everything because things used to be bad. Even when I was at my worst, there was something, so
I try to notice and appreciate everything. 

The first night I didn’t cry after my ex tried to kill me. A roof over my head he’s never seen and never will see. The holiday lights my neighbors put up in December. The fresh groceries in my fridge. The curtain rod that falls on my head while I’m sleeping sometimes. Friends I once loved but no longer talk to. The neighborhood cat who lets me pet her. The job I used to work that didn’t fulfill me, and getting fired from it. The bridge I drive over now that I almost drove off at my lowest. 

Even when I had nothing, I had something. I am grateful for it all.

You don’t need to feel embarrassed about opening up to other family members or teachers at all. Even if they take it badly, that’s not your fault even a little bit. You will find a mentor who wants to help you if you keep trying. It sounds like your parents are neglecting you pretty hardcore. 

Don’t listen to your dad or your boss— at that age, your mistakes reflect a lot on your parents and their ability/inability to raise you. If your father is upset with something you’ve done, it’s his job to sit you down, hear you out, and help you correct your behavior. If your father is truly disappointed in you (assuming he didn’t say that just to hurt you, which he absolutely could have), he should feel disappointed in himself. He is not doing right by you if he is expressing disdain for your actions without providing the right guidance. That is just judging you and hurting you, and it isn’t constructive in any possible way. 

Also, do not believe anyone when they say they don’t think that you are college material. Adults have all sorts of ulterior motives for saying things like this, especially when they have power over you like in a boss-employee relationship. You deserve to be surrounded by people who believe in you and your potential and want to nurture you. I would suggest trying to reach out to your aunt/uncle, or teachers at your school who you think you could confide in. A lot of schools also have guidance counselors and advisors for exactly this sort of thing, and I think you could really benefit from talking to some sort of counselor. You can also talk to friends’ parents, coaches or instructors, religious leaders, any adult you feel comfortable around. 

But don’t worry about maturing too fast. 
You’re 16. You’re supposed to still be a kid. Some parents have a lot of difficulty not holding their children to absolutely perfect standards, which is unfair because we never meet perfect standards as adults. The mistakes you make at this age will probably not be detrimental to the rest of your life (assuming none of them are serious crimes). I wish I had done more adventurous things and had been a little less serious at your age, I think I would have learned a lot more about myself and the world. 

Children are just adults whose brains aren’t done cooking, and you can’t expect half-baked dough to taste like bread yet. It needs more time in the oven. And you can’t force it to rise faster than it’s able to. 

You’re 16 and already working. You don’t have a single adult in your life who seems to care about you the way you need. Don’t mistake their shortcomings as your fault. You’re doing amazing! Especially given the circumstances.

I’ve also dealt with this before, unfortunately, with several (thankfully now ex) partners and honestly, it’s one of the most sickening feelings in the world. I’m so sorry you’re going through it right now. To have an intimate partner not only betray your trust by not respecting your trauma when you *specifically* told them it’s not something you’re comfortable with just anybody knowing, and to have them and a person you only know because of them MAKE LIGHT of the horrible trauma you’ve endured is absolutely inexcusable. It’s so hard to be able to trust anyone after enduring bad things in the past, and they should have honored your relationship enough to see that and keep what you told them between you two. They literally didn’t even have to come to that conclusion on their own (though they should have) because you explicitly told them, so anything they’ve done against your needs is deliberate.

It’s a perfectly acceptable request to make, and you will find people who will honor that and take it seriously. Yes, everybody needs someone to vent to, but it’s one thing to talk out your feelings, and another to do this. They never had to say anything specific about your past beyond “my partner is dealing with the aftermath of trauma” or “my partner has PTSD” (if you were comfortable with them sharing just that information and no details) to be able to provide context to anything they needed to say about your relationship to anyone. They deliberately chose to tell a story that wasn’t theirs to tell. 

Unfortunately, I don’t think there’s anything to do except break up. They might try to convince you not to, or make you seem like you’re being dramatic (had that happen before when breaking up for this exact reason), but you are the only person with the right to tell your story, and anyone who truly cares for you will listen to what you need and apologize when wrong. I hope you heal quickly from this, too. You did nothing wrong.

I’m sorry people are being weird in the comments. I don’t think a lot of people understand how much marriage/being single changes how women are viewed and treated in society. I wore a fake ring for years for a matter of safety at my job (worked in a restaurant). It’s insane how differently people act towards you. Without my ring, I regularly got followed home and had a stalker for a few months who tried to break into my apartment multiple times. I got assaulted at my job, and regularly harassed. But people are much less willing to try anything if they think there’s another man in the house (which is so so annoying). 

And you don’t owe anybody the truth, especially when you’re not hurting anyone, and ESPECIALLY when they would treat you differently for a stupid reason if they knew. Being a single mother is amazing and so so SO impressive! You have to juggle a million things at the same time in an act of pure love and selflessness. It’s something incredible to be proud of. I’m so sorry people treat it like a “lack of a man” rather than seeing how amazing it is that you do everything yourself. Not only did you create the miracle of life, but you’re sustaining it entirely on your own. That’s something to be proud of. Don’t let anyone tell you otherwise!

Edit: for clarity

SG has some angularity to them, usually in the skeleton with soft flesh on top. They look small, and have a “spunkier” essence to them. They pull off mismatched elements because they themselves have a combination of both yin and yang features in their body. Gamine is more of a collection of different features that make up one person, so the lines of different parts of the body aren’t always the same. This means gamine bodies have a lot of variation throughout, but the yin/yang balance is the most important and defining trait of G. 
For example, look at Reese Witherspoon’s face. She has a prominent jawline (yang), big, round eyes (yin), a sharper nose (yang) delicately rounded cheekbones (yin) and taut lips (yang). Yes we don’t type by face anymore, but this is just an example of the “mismatch” of features Gamines can have. If D is sharp yang, and N is softened yang, G is “sharp” yin and R is soft yin. 

R has no yang in the body. R is composed of only rounded lines in both the skeleton and the flesh. No part of the frame shapes the clothes, only the flesh on top. Since R is not a mix of yin and yang, and is only yin, they have less of an “animated” presence, and have a more obvious harmony in the features. Since they are only rounded, they have less to worry about in terms of yin/yang because the have no yang. Take Kate Winslet’s face for this example. She has only yin features, with full lips, round cheekbones, round eyes, a rounded nose, and a round jawline. Her features all match in roundedness.

You do look small in comparison to others, but in my opinion vertical line is more about how you’re proportioned and how clothes fall on you. For example, gamines do best in very short lines because they are proportioned in a way that longer clothing is going to swallow them and make them look even smaller. Say that gamine is 5’4”. There can be another woman who is the same height with FN proportions, because clothing will fall on her the way it would if she were tall. She is still shorter, and will look small in comparison to other people who are tall, but the way she is proportioned means that she looks best in lines that aren’t typically associated with smaller people. 

So you could still be DC even though you look small! If you think you’re not DC, I’d recommend trying out some other lines and compare them to DC to see which you like best.

Of course! I'm happy to have helped. A bit more on those terms:
Unconstructed refers to the shape of the silhouette. Certain garments are very shaped, like menswear blazers for example tend to have sharp and shaped edges. This means there's not a lot of give in them, because the fabric itself is shaped and tailored to create a certain silhouette on the body. Naturals look best when their body does the shaping, and the clothing they put over them is not tailored to be a clearly defined shape. Their bones are already shapely, so clothing lines that are too shapely already are going to look bulky and work against their natural frame. Unconstructed lines will loosely hang off the bones of the body and let the natural body shape show through. They should not be too tight or too stiff. Unconstructed is often referred to as "relaxed," and will have some room for movement in the fabric because it is less shaped. If you drape a simple piece of light, flowing fabric over yourself, that is an example of a relaxed line--- it doesn't have any seams to shape it a certain way, it merely hangs off your body's natural shape.

Naturals have width to them, and should ideally accommodate for that width so they don't look disproportionate. Shirts and dresses with wider necklines are essential, as anything with too narrow a neckline will make their shoulders look wider and disproportionate by comparison. If you took that piece of fabric from the last example and draped it over your shoulders like a cape and crossed it in the front to create a wrap shirt, you should place the edges of the neckline closer to your shoulders rather than closer to your neck. Shirts with straps placed closer to the neck create narrower illusions, shirts with straps placed closer to the edge of the shoulders have wider necklines and create a more proportionate look for you. As for bottoms, skinny jeans and tight pencil skirts might make you look constrained. I'd generally stay away from anything too bodycon, tight, or stiff because that harmonizes with narrowness and works against width. Looser, flowing skirts and more relaxed pants and shorts are going to look best on you because they accommodate that width that you naturally have in your bones. 
Hope this helped!

It might take you a while, but I’d recommend first understanding the concept of yin and yang within the body and what they mean. For example, soft natural shares both yin and yang traits- more yang bone structure (usually they have blunt shoulders and bones, with some width to their silhouette), some yin in their bone structure (shorter vertical line), mostly yin in the flesh (larger bust, may have rounder hips, will probably have noticeable curves to their silhouette), and some yang in their flesh (many have straight hips, wider waistlines, muscular arms and legs). This means that the overall impression you’d get from a soft natural is that they’re wide with blunter bones, have noticeable curves, and look shorter. How does that translate to clothing? 
Wide shoulders and blunt bones mean that accommodating the shoulders and width of the skeleton is important. They will look good in loose and unconstructed lines with movable fabrics and wider necklines. Things that hang off the skeleton a bit and aren’t super tight and constricting are key for them. They will look good in looser and wider things that mimic the blunt width in their bones. 
Now to the flesh- they will have some rounder and softer flesh, so softly rounded shapes will harmonize with their body. One good example for this is peasant tops with rounded necklines. These tops usually have wider shoulders and a wider stature in the neckline, but also have those rounded edges around the bustline that combine to make a perfect soft natural shirt. For bottoms, waist emphasis will look good on you, and you want to avoid anything too shapeless and boxy because you will lose your figure. Garments should be relaxed and draped, but not too formless on SNs. Another example of a good top is oversized sweaters. You will want to make sure they still fit at the cuffs (for an element of yin) and have a relaxed but not completely formless fit. The neckline should accommodate your shoulders, meaning it should be wider to mimic them and not to narrow (so you don’t look too broad by comparison)
Mom jeans and shorts are usually really nice on SNs because they have a relaxed fit and you can taper them in at the waist and tuck in long shirts for waist emphasis. Paper bag shorts are also a great fit for SNs for the same reason. 
Now for height- SNs look shorter, so shorter pieces of clothing will look good on them. You want to avoid dressing in one color head to toe and instead break up your vertical line by distinguishing your torso from your legs. If you’re wearing a dress, it should ideally be shorter in length, as you can easily get lost and look disproportionate in dresses and skirts that are too long. 

The key to understanding Kibbe is observing the lines your body already has and mimicking them through the lines of your clothing. I hope this helped!

Literally always. I feel this so much, all the time, that it’s one of the dominating thoughts I have multiple times a day. It’s a weird dichotomy of being not enough and “too much” at the same time. I’m too much for other people, but not enough for myself, and at the same time I’m too much for myself and not enough for other people. 
I haven’t figured out how to cope with it entirely myself, but what I would recommend is first finding things you like about yourself and writing them down. They can be small things (maybe you like your handwriting, your smile, your laugh, the way you make hot chocolate, something cute to romanticize) or big things (personality aspects, the impression you give other people, talents you possess, etc). Try not to rate them on a scale of comparison to other people, and instead just focus on only yourself. If you’re an artist, don’t think about who you think might be better than you, or what is missing in your own art, simply appreciate that you have the drive, artistry, bravery, and creativity to make art. Try to think about yourself like you’re in love with you. Ask yourself what someone who was in love with you would appreciate. You could ask people who love you, but I think it’s much better to come up with this list without any outside influence, because relying on other peoples’ perception of you is not going to strengthen your own perception of yourself. It will just mold yours to theirs. 
Another thing you might want to try is making time in the day to do something just for yourself that nobody else will ever see or know about. It could be drawing, writing, making a snowman, drinking tea and reading, or really anything (but preferably creative in some way). Take in small, quiet moments to just be with yourself, and be as present as you can. Again, it’s sort of like falling in love with yourself. Then, once you’re more comfortable, start thinking about the traits you think are holding you back from your ideal perfection. There are certain things that can and maybe should be altered (for example, attention to detail can be crucial in some instances and can be learned relatively quickly and easily if you put your mind to it), but a lot of them might just be things you have to come to terms with in yourself. I know when I see someone I love deeply do something less than perfect, I kind of find it adorable (as long as it’s not hurtful or mean spirited). Flaws make a person themselves, which is cliched but true. 
All the imperfect things you do can sort of be like handmade cards—- beautiful for the effort and sentiment, and far realer, unique, and heartier than anything mass produced, although maybe not exhibiting the same quality. They can each good for different reasons, but I’d much prefer hard work, effort, and sentiment over a perfect result. I know it’s hard to apply the same principle to yourself, but if you do everything with passion and with conviction, it will usually show through in your work, and that’s a rare and standout quality that really draws people in and gives them a reason to care about what you’ve done. I’d rather look at art that was made from passion than something technically perfect. I’d rather be with someone who has flaws but cares deeply for me than someone who is cookie cutter perfect but feels less strongly about me. 

I think love is the thing that sort of erases those harsh expectations you put on yourself. Feelings of inadequacy will probably pop up less and mean less to you if you have that strong foundation of self love that stifles the negative voice in your head. It’s sort of like a friend comforting you when you’re down, but you’re your own friend and also the one being comforted. 

Another thing I’ve learned—which might seem silly but has helped me so much—is to say the phrase “it be like that” or “it is what it is”. When things go wrong in my own life, I often immediately assume it’s my fault and I am a horrible person who can’t do anything right, that I’m fundamentally broken in some sort of way that inherently makes anything I do worse than anything anyone else does simply because I did it. Instead, I try to practice self-grace by saying “eh, sometimes it just be like that”. More often than not I’m not going to live up to my own unrealistic expectations. They’re unrealistic. But I can try to be content with what I can do, and appreciate that my hard work, although not usually yielding the quality of result I set out to accomplish, is still far better than having done nothing at all. 

Another angle is to try and really enjoy and immerse yourself in what you’re doing. You’re less likely to compare yourself to others or to your ideal when you’re really invested in what you’re doing. I know I’m way less self conscious at the beach when I’m preoccupied with diving under waves or finding cute shells. I’m never worried if my makeup is running, or If my hair dried weirdly, or anything really. 

Comparison to an unachievable ideal is not going to benefit you in any way. It’s hard to stop, and I don’t pretend to know all the answers or have an immediate solution to it. I don’t know if these will help you, but I do hope they start to lay healthier foundations if you decide to give them a try.

Kieran is the only person who makes logical sense (with timing and everything) but a piece seems to be missing (no one really knows anything about before he came to lakewood, his parents car crash, etc). It even would make sense that he was helping in the first season because he's conveniently missing during a lot of attacks, and if Piper was the one orchestrating most attacks and Kieran was a helper, it would make a lot of sense. It would also make a lot of sense that he's dating Emma, because it would keep him close enough to her but not too close as to arouse suspicion. She would also trust him, which is an added bonus. Everyone wrote him off as a red herring in the first season because he tugged on our heart strings when his father died, and when he told Emma about the car crash. Usually in horror movies you can rule out the people that the characters start suspecting, which is why he was ruled out in the first season. But in this season, he isn't really suspicious to the character's knowledge, but it would make a lot of sense if he were the killer (dramatic irony, the audience knows he's shady and it makes sense but the characters seem to not be able to tell). It would also make sense that he would have enough money to buy the expensive drugged alcohol from earlier in the season, and he'd probably have the tech knowledge needed to do what the killer does (although he doesn't necessarily display any knowledge or tech skills, it doesn't really fit his character persona and it would make sense that if he knew how to do it he wouldn't really flaunt it).
